sections.heading: Point estimates for the population mean

questions.q: A sample of $6$ measurements has values $14,18,12,16,15,17$. Find the unbiased point estimate of the population mean.
Explain why the unbiased estimator of population variance, $s^2=\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2$, divides by $n-1$ rather than $n$.
questions.answer: Dividing by $n$ would systematically underestimate the true population variance on average, since $\bar{x}$ is computed from the same sample, making squared deviations from $\bar{x}$ slightly smaller than deviations from the true (unknown) population mean $\mu$. Dividing by $n-1$ (the degrees of freedom) corrects this bias.

questions.q: A sample of $n=8$ has $\sum x_i=152$. Find $\bar{x}$, the unbiased point estimate of $\mu$.
For the sample $5,8,10,7,10$, find the unbiased estimate of the population variance.
questions.answer: Mean $=\dfrac{5+8+10+7+10}{5}=8$. Squared deviations: $9,0,4,1,4$, summing to $18$. $s^2=\dfrac{18}{5-1}=4.5$.

questions.q: A sample of $n=10$ has $\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2=81$. Find the unbiased estimate of the population variance and standard deviation, to three decimal places.
For the sample $12,9,14,11,13,15$, find the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, to three decimal places.
State the Central Limit Theorem as it applies to the sample mean $\bar{X}$ of a random sample of size $n$ from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$.
questions.answer: For sufficiently large $n$, $\bar{X}$ is approximately normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution — this holds even if the underlying population is not normal, provided $n$ is large enough (a common guideline is $n\geq30$).

questions.q: A population has mean $\mu=40$ and standard deviation $\sigma=12$. A random sample of size $n=36$ is taken. Using the Central Limit Theorem, state the approximate distribution of $\bar{X}$.
questions.answer: $\bar{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$ approximately, with $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}=\dfrac{144}{36}=4$. So $\bar{X}\sim N(40,4)$ approximately, i.e. mean $40$, standard deviation $2$.

questions.q: Explain why the Central Limit Theorem is so useful in practice, even when the underlying population distribution is unknown or non-normal.
questions.answer: It allows normal-distribution-based methods (confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for $\mu$) to be used even without knowing the population's exact distribution shape, as long as the sample size is reasonably large — making inference about $\mu$ possible in a very wide range of real-world situations.

sections.heading: Using the distribution of the sample mean

questions.q: Using $\bar{X}\sim N(40,4)$ from above, find $P(\bar{X}>43)$, given $\Phi(1.5)\approx0.9332$.
Using the same distribution, find $P(38<\bar{X}<41)$, given $\Phi(0.5)\approx0.6915$ and $\Phi(-1)\approx0.1587$.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals for μ with known σ

questions.q: A sample of $n=49$ has mean $\bar{x}=68$ and known population standard deviation $\sigma=7$. Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$, using $z^*=1.96$.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{49}}=1$. Margin of error: $1.96(1)=1.96$. Confidence interval: $68\pm1.96$, or $(66.04,69.96)$.

questions.q: A sample of $n=64$ has mean $\bar{x}=25$ and $\sigma=8$. Construct a 90% confidence interval for $\mu$, using $z^*=1.645$.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{64}}=1$. Margin of error: $1.645(1)=1.645$. Confidence interval: $25\pm1.645$, or $(23.355,26.645)$.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals with unknown σ (large samples)

questions.q: A sample of $n=100$ has mean $\bar{x}=52.4$ and sample standard deviation $s=9$. Since $n$ is large, construct a 99% confidence interval for $\mu$ using $z^*=2.576$ as an approximation, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{100}}=0.9$. Margin of error: $2.576(0.9)\approx2.3184$. Confidence interval: $52.4\pm2.32$, or approximately $(50.08,54.72)$.

questions.q: A sample of $n=50$ has mean $\bar{x}=110$ and sample standard deviation $s=15$. Construct a 90% confidence interval for $\mu$, using $z^*=1.645$, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\dfrac{15}{\sqrt{50}}\approx2.1213$. Margin of error: $1.645(2.1213)\approx3.49$. Confidence interval: $110\pm3.49$, or approximately $(106.51,113.49)$.

questions.q: A researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$ with margin of error at most $1.5$, given $\sigma=10$. Find the minimum sample size, using $z^*=1.96$, rounding up.
questions.answer: $n=\left(\dfrac{z^*\sigma}{E}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{1.96(10)}{1.5}\right)^2\approx(13.067)^2\approx170.74$. Rounding up: $n=171$.

questions.q: A researcher wants a 99% confidence interval for $\mu$ with margin of error at most $3$, given $\sigma=15$. Find the minimum sample size, using $z^*=2.576$, rounding up.
A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is $(41.2,48.8)$. State the correct interpretation of this interval.
questions.answer: If this sampling and interval-construction process were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population mean. It is NOT correct to say there is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this specific interval, since the true mean is a fixed (though unknown) value, not a random variable.

questions.q: Explain why increasing the confidence level from 90% to 99%, with the sample data unchanged, produces a wider confidence interval.
questions.answer: A higher confidence level requires a larger critical value $z^*$ (approximately $2.576$ for 99% versus $1.645$ for 90%). Since the margin of error is directly proportional to $z^*$, a larger $z^*$ produces a wider interval — there is an inherent tradeoff between confidence level and precision.

sections.heading: A well-designed word problem: estimating average commute time

questions.q: This question has four parts. A researcher surveys $n=64$ randomly selected commuters, finding sample mean commute time $\bar{x}=34.5$ minutes with sample standard deviation $s=12$ minutes. (a) State the unbiased point estimate of the population mean commute time. (b) Since $n$ is large, construct a 95% confidence interval for the true mean, using $z^*=1.96$. (c) The city claims the average commute is $30$ minutes. Using your confidence interval, comment on whether this claim is plausible. (d) The researcher wants a margin of error of at most $2$ minutes at the same confidence level. Find the minimum required sample size, using $s=12$ as an estimate of $\sigma$, rounding up.
questions.answer: (a) $34.5$ minutes. (b) Standard error: $\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{64}}=1.5$. Margin of error: $1.96(1.5)=2.94$. Confidence interval: $34.5\pm2.94$, or $(31.56,37.44)$. (c) Since $30$ minutes lies outside this interval (below the lower bound of $31.56$), there is evidence at the 95% confidence level that the true mean commute time exceeds the city's claimed $30$ minutes — the claim is not well supported by the data. (d) $n=\left(\dfrac{1.96(12)}{2}\right)^2=(11.76)^2\approx138.30$. Rounding up: $n=139$.
